title: Anthropic Says It Blocked Russian Bid to Build Killer Drone Swarm
excerpt: The company says a Russia-based group used Claude to engineer autonomous drones able to pick targets — including people — and detonate without human approval.
body:
• Anthropic says it disrupted a Russia-based operation that used its Claude AI to engineer software for an autonomous swarm of kamikaze drones — capable of selecting targets, including people, and detonating without human involvement.
  • The group, tracked as GTG-27005, built shared swarm memory, an onboard language model to govern attack decisions, and terminal guidance to steer drones to targets. The system was never deployed to the field.
  • Anthropic described the freelance developers as a small team likely tied to a regional university and a Russian Academy of Sciences research centre; it could not verify their claims of funding from Russian defence research bodies.
  • The disclosure came in a 154-page report on misuse of Claude, which also details disrupted attempts by Chinese and Yemeni groups to use the AI for weapons design, plus cyberattack and disinformation campaigns.

Anthropic has revealed that it blocked a Russia-based operation attempting to use its Claude artificial intelligence system to build the software core of an autonomous kamikaze drone swarm — a system designed, the company said, to select targets and detonate without a human in the loop.

The disclosure appeared in a 154-page Anthropic report on malicious use of Claude in state-sponsored operations. A small freelance group of Russia-based developers — tracked as GTG-27005 — used Claude Code to write, test and store code for first-person-view (FPV) "kamikaze" drones able to independently select targets and crash into them to detonate explosives.

What the group built

With Claude's help, the group developed shared swarm memory and fault-tolerant coordination logic so multiple drones could operate together; an onboard small language model to govern whether drones should attack, observe or return to base; a terminal guidance system to steer drones to targets using the onboard camera and issue the detonation command; a control-link geolocation module to locate opposing drone operators; and a passive acoustic detection layer.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2099469039382696385

The platform, the company said, was "designed for autonomous lethal engagement," with target classes that explicitly included "person."

"[The system was] designed for autonomous lethal engagement," with target classes that explicitly included "person."

— Anthropic, in its report on malicious use of Claude

The developers trained a computer-vision classifier on scraped Ukrainian combat footage, labelling targets "friendly" or "enemy" and placing Russian systems on the friendly list. They repeatedly used the same coordinates in Ukraine's Donetsk region as a demonstration strike point.

How it was caught

The operation, dubbed "DronDoc" or "Serafim," began in mid-May 2026. The accounts linked to it were created between late 2025 and early 2026, and the developers bypassed Anthropic's geographic restrictions by routing traffic through commercial virtual private servers.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=QA9tf5zU1SQ

While the Russian group had not yet deployed the model to the field, it was doing "real hardware-in-loop testing" within its sessions, according to the report — meaning the software was being tested against physical drone hardware. Anthropic banned nine accounts linked to the group, incorporated the findings into its safeguards, and shared details with industry groups.

Anthropic concluded the group was a small freelance team handling civilian and military contracts rather than an organisation directly tied to the Russian government, though members appeared tied to a regional university and a Russian Academy of Sciences research centre. The developers claimed funding from Russia's Advanced Research Foundation, a DARPA-like state defence body — claims Anthropic could not independently verify.

Part of a wider pattern

The drone-swarm case was not the report's only Russia finding. Anthropic also described how foreign groups used Claude in elaborate data theft and disinformation campaigns — digging up information on targets, finding vulnerabilities in online accounts, creating malware to steal data, and building networks of fake social media profiles and entire news sites. Reuters reported that one hacking group's tactics resembled those of the Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard, which the US government has previously linked to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. The company also said it disrupted attempts by Chinese and Yemeni groups to use Claude to design conventional weapons.

What it means

Small FPV drones have become one of the defining weapons of the war in Ukraine, with both sides using them extensively. Anthropic's disclosure is the latest warning from AI firms and think tanks that made-in-America AI tools are being turned into weapons by Russia, China, Iran and others — and a test case for whether AI companies can detect and stop misuse before it reaches the battlefield. The system never made it there. The next one might.
nri_angle: The weaponisation of Western AI by Russia is a core geopolitical story for a diaspora readership that follows the Ukraine war, India-Russia ties, and the AI safety debate closely.
